t: #3997 Count Dominant Nodes in a Binary Tree
o: A node is dominant when its value equals the maximum value anywhere in its own subtree. Every leaf is automatically dominant (its subtree max is itself). In Example 1, four leaves plus the node 8 (whose subtree max is 8) give 5. In Example 2, three leaves plus the node 2 (subtree [2,1,2], max 2) give 4. The computation is a textbook post-order traversal: compute each subtree's maximum bottom-up, and increment a counter whenever a node's value ties that maximum. With up to 1e5 nodes, an O(n) traversal is required; the tree being complete only bounds the depth (~log n), so even recursion is safe, though an iterative version avoids any recursion-limit concerns.
k: A leaf is always dominant; internal nodes are dominant exactly when their value >= both children's subtree maxima.
Subtree maximum can be computed bottom-up in one pass: max(node.val, max(left subtree max, right subtree max)).
Any O(n) tree traversal works; the complete-tree guarantee keeps depth logarithmic, so recursion depth is not an issue.

a.i: Each recursive call returns the maximum value of its subtree and increments a global counter when the current node's value equals that maximum. Null children contribute negative infinity so they never affect the comparison.
s: Define dfs(node) returning the subtree maximum.
Recurse on left and right children; take max(node.val, leftMax, rightMax).
If node.val equals this maximum, increment the answer counter.
Return the counter after calling dfs(root).
a.t: O(n) — each node is visited exactly once during the post-order traversal.
a.sp: O(h) recursion stack, h = O(log n) for a complete tree.

a.n: Approach 2: Iterative Post-order with Explicit Stack
a.i: Same logic, but simulate the call stack explicitly with (node, processed) pairs: push children first, and when a node is popped the second time its children's subtree maxima are already recorded in a map keyed by node reference. This eliminates recursion entirely, useful in languages/environments with shallow stacks.
s: Push (root, false) onto a stack; keep a map from node id to subtree max.
On popping an unprocessed node, push (node, true) then its children (unprocessed).
On popping a processed node, compute max of its value and its children's recorded maxima; store it and count dominance.
a.t: O(n) — each node is pushed twice (once unprocessed, once processed).
a.sp: O(n) for the stack and the map of subtree maxima.

w: Prefer the recursive DFS in an interview — it is three lines of core logic; mention the iterative variant if asked about deep trees or stack limits. Pitfalls: forgetting that leaves are dominant (handled naturally by treating null as -infinity), and comparing against children incorrectly (must compare against the full subtree max, which for a node equals max of itself and both children's results). Follow-ups: count nodes dominant over the entire tree instead of their subtree (a preorder running-max pass), or return the sum of values of dominant nodes.
